before.exam_tip_html: For the specified-poem question on “The Schoolboy,” always explain how the caged-bird metaphor works before you assert what it means — examiners reward analysis of how imagery creates its effect, not just naming the technique. For the comparison question, choose a pairing poem you can quote confidently, since the anthology is closed book: Wordsworth’s daffodils or Clarke’s “Catrin” both give you short, memorable quotations to set against Blake’s.

When writing about Act 1, compare the two love stories from the start. Claudio’s visual, transactional love (“In mine eye she is the sweetest lady”) versus Beatrice and Benedick’s verbal, combative connection. Examiners reward students who explain how Shakespeare structures the play around this contrast and why it matters for the themes of appearance versus reality.

St John is an underused character in exam responses. If your extract touches on Moor House or St John’s proposal, analyse how Brontë uses him as a foil to Rochester: both offer Jane incomplete relationships. Show how Jane’s refusal of St John parallels her departure from Thornfield, proving that her moral standards are consistent. This structural awareness impresses examiners.

If discussing the ending, consider multiple interpretations. Is Rochester’s blindness a necessary condition for equality, or a punishment for deception? Is the retreat to Ferndean freedom or escape? Examiners reward responses that explore complexity rather than settling for a single reading. Use ‘some critics argue’ and ‘alternatively’ to show you can evaluate different perspectives.

Symbolism is prime AO2 material. First select specific images from the printed extract (the tape, the fence, the boat) and analyse their layered meanings — what they represent literally, emotionally, and thematically. Then trace how a symbol develops across the novel: the tape appears in three key scenes (Kathy as a child, Norfolk replacement, Madame’s explanation), and its meaning deepens each time. Examiners reward students who track symbolism through the whole text, not just in one passage.

The drama question is worth 40 marks, and the paper gives you two and a half hours for three sections, so plan on about 50 minutes. Aim for three detailed analytical points on the printed extract with embedded quotations, then three more from different parts of the play. Every paragraph should contain a point about Priestley’s purpose, a quotation and analysis of language or structure. Check your spelling and punctuation as you go, because accurate writing carries marks here. The examiner is looking for ‘how Priestley presents’ — always foreground the writer’s choices.

For the specified-poem question on ‘Kamikaze’, examiners want you to explore the shift between the natural imagery of the sea and the harsh, silent world of the family — don’t just describe the plot. For the comparison question, always explain the method behind each short quotation (form, structure, or specific word choice) rather than simply stating what happens in both poems.

This is a closed-book exam, so memorise short, exact quotations rather than whole lines — “probably armed, possibly not,” “sort of inside out” and “bloody life in my bloody hands” are all compact enough to recall precisely under pressure. If ‘Remains’ is the specified poem, spend real time on form and structure, not just content — examiners reward comment on caesura, enjambment and the colloquial voice. If it appears in the comparison question, choose a partner poem you know well (Kamikaze, War Photographer or Disabled) and plan your comparison around shared methods, not just shared subject matter.
